title: The Hackett-Dickenson Roosevelt Grill album and Hank O'Neal's liner notes
summary: Leeman recommends the 1977 Chiaroscuro album recorded in 1970 and reads liner notes saying the tunes are not Dixieland but tasteful swing.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: my sake, try this album for sound. This LP album is available; it's called Bobby Hackett featuring Vic Dickenson at the Roosevelt Grill.
Now I find this rather hard to pronounce; always have -- it says 1977 Chiaroscuro Records, a division of Audio-Fidelity Enterprises, 221 West 57th Street, New York 10019.

We made four or five albums at this time. This particular album has a picture of a steaming trumpet on it, or a clarinet, rather, and the steam coming out of the spit valve, and there's an old fashioned fireman on the ladder blowing one of those old fish horns. That's just to identify this particular record.

Now the songs, just to make sure, are Fidgety Feet, 'Baby Won't You Please Come Home,' 'Wait on the New Orleans,' 'Tin Blues,' 'Sweet Georgia Brown,' 'After You've Gone,' New Orleans, 'Struttin' at the Barbecue,' 'Basin Street Blues' and 'Wolverine Blues.'

And there are some most interesting notes here, that Hank O'Neal who recorded and produced it wrote down. It starts off -- and I'm only going to take a couple of them here -- "I hate Dixieland jazz, at least I hate the kind of rubbish people play." In '77, they called it Dixieland.
Later on, he goes on to say "Why am I putting out an album with all these Dixieland tunes on it?" A good question, and an easy answer. It isn't Dixieland. Thank
God. When Bobby first made these recordings in '70, I programmed two albums, and I bought one and kept the other.

In 1970, we recorded ten nights, and produced a gigantic pile of tapes. There was an awful lot of material there, when the albums were programmed, because in my preconceived notion of the truth, I rejected all of the tunes with Dixieland titles, except one -- I never listened to them.

Listening to them now, however, I was surprised to find they were not Dixieland at all, but just good, swinging songs with Bobby, Vic, Dave, Jack and Cliff. Being as tasty as they could be -- a real revelation. I kept listening carefully, and in most instances, the selections are not only spirited, but played flawlessly. And being somewhat easy to play 'Sweet Georgia Brown' than a difficult ballad. These were just good songs being played sensibly. What a relief.

Later the guys who played these tunes the same way every time and every night in 1961 at Ryan's and other places, should give these tunes a listen, and realize what time and tone and taste can do for a song. A tune, rather.

I want to stress that I'm not trying to sell albums, but for the student who might be interested in my progression as a drummer and my different expressions in playing, might find this as an example of what I tried to bring forth before -- and not the epitome of my playing, but I
enjoyed the sound, the different sounds that I got on the drum solos, and I would like to convey this and pass it along to somebody who may be interested.
